activities.anchor: That square root is why polls cost what they cost
activities.caption: the count vs the draw — drag the divider
activities.name: ssCostCompare

config.prompt: Two things a poll's budget can buy — drag the divider:

before.label: what the count buys
before.text: a bigger n buys less and less: halving the margin of error takes four times the interviews

after.label: what the draw decides
after.text: whether the sample speaks for its population at all — a big non-random count is noise with a big number attached

config.why: Representativeness is a property of the method, never of the count.

activities.anchor: Sample size multiplies whatever the method already is
activities.caption: true or false — can size rescue a draw?
activities.name: ssSizeJudge

statements.s: Bias is a systematic tilt, not noise.
statements.why: A tilt points the same way in every observation; noise points randomly and cancels on average.

statements.s: Averaging more biased data averages the tilt more precisely.
statements.why: More data narrows the estimate around the wrong target.

statements.s: A big enough sample eventually fixes a biased draw.
statements.why: The bias lives in the selection mechanism; growth just repeats it with tighter error bars.

activities.anchor: One term does the quiet work in between
activities.caption: the vocabulary — pair each term with its job
activities.name: ssVocabMatch

config.prompt: Match each term to what it names:

pairs.right: everyone the question is about — all voters, all oak trees, every bolt in a production run
slow, ruinously expensive, strains to reach everyone — and more enumerators means more chances to err
the actual list you draw from — a school register, a phone directory, an electoral roll

config.why: The frame and the population are rarely the same thing — and that gap is where the first bias enters.

activities.anchor: national polls cluster around 1,000 to 2,000 respondents
activities.caption: bet on the margin of error
activities.name: ssNPredict

config.q: The same well-drawn poll of a thousand people runs on a country of 3 million and one of 300 million. Which carries the smaller margin of error?
choices: The small country — the sample is a bigger fraction of it
The large country — more diversity needs more sample
Essentially the same — the margin depends on n, not N
Impossible to say without the exact population figures
config.why: Essentially the same, roughly ±3 points in both — the absolute count sets the margin, not the size of the population it stands for.

activities.anchor: The same job is done by
activities.caption: the random-number-table procedure, in order
activities.name: ssTableOrder

config.prompt: A school of 864, a sample of 30 — order the procedure:
items: Number the students 001 to 864 — all three-digit numbers
Enter the table of random digits anywhere — the starting point must itself be arbitrary
Read digits in groups of three: 402, 781, 937, 056, 223, 990, 114 …
Keep 402, 781, 056, 223, 114; skip 937 and 990 — no student carries those numbers; skip any repeat
config.why: The requirement is not the tool but the equal, known chance for every member — decided by chance machinery, not by anyone's convenience.

activities.caption: one line of the method guide is wrong — click it
activities.name: ssMethodSpot

config.prompt: One line of this methods guide is wrong — click it:
lines: Systematic: for 864 students and a sample of 30, choose every 29th after a random start among the first 29.
It is cheap and spreads evenly across the frame.
It stays effectively random even when the list has a repeating pattern aligned with the interval.
Stratified: split the frame into strata that matter, sample each in proportion, draw randomly within.
Quota: interviewers fill instructed quotas, choosing whom to ask — fast, cheap, and needing no frame.
config.correction: A repeating pattern aligned with the interval is exactly where systematic breaks: every 29th house on a street whose blocks repeat every 30 is a self-inflicted wound.
config.why: Quota re-imports the bias randomness exists to remove — approachable people get asked — making it stratification without the random step.

activities.caption: what weighting repairs vs what it cannot — drag the divider
activities.name: ssWeightCompare

config.prompt: The poll came in light on one group. Drag the divider:

before.label: what weighting repairs
before.text: composition: adjust age, sex, region and education until they match known population figures, boosting the groups the draw missed — the fix that pulled election polling back on track in 2016

after.label: what weighting cannot repair
after.text: the frame itself — no weighting rescues a draw whose list never contained part of the population

config.why: A repair, not a substitute for a good draw.

activities.anchor: the frame, not the map, defines the population
activities.caption: probability or non-probability? file the draw
activities.name: ssFrameSort

config.prompt: Two families of sample — file each draw:

items.label: multi-stage national designs: regions, neighbourhoods, addresses, one respondent

config.why: The margin of error printed under a poll is a promise about probability sampling from a named list; precision no formula can certify belongs in the other bucket.

activities.caption: you are pilot-testing the questionnaire — walk the desk
activities.name: ssQBranch

config.root: A questionnaire lands on your desk for the pilot. Walk the traps.

start.text: “Don't you agree the canteen food is terrible?”

choices.label: Flag it — a leading question
choices.feedback: It embeds the conclusion; rewrite it balanced, both directions equally phrased.

choices.label: Keep it — it is short
choices.feedback: Short, and it manufactures agreement rather than measuring it.

lead.text: Next: “Are you satisfied with the price and quality of the food?”

choices.label: Flag it — double-barrelled
choices.feedback: Which one? Split it into two questions, each measuring a single thing.

choices.label: Keep it — two answers for one
choices.feedback: The respondent cannot tell you which half they meant.

choices.label: Flag it — overlapping options
choices.feedback: A 20-year-old fits two bands: the overlap double-counts and manufactures phantom respondents.

choices.label: Keep it — everyone fits somewhere
choices.feedback: Everyone fits twice — that is the defect.

fixed.text: Cleared for the field: exhaustive and balanced options, one question per topic, non-overlapping bands — then randomise question order where priming is a risk.

kept.text: The questionnaire now manufactures answers — leading wording, double barrels and overlaps all push in whatever direction the writing leaned.

config.why: Closed questions must be exhaustive and balanced; the pilot remains the cheapest defect detector ever invented.
